structure.title: Defence
structure.text: Socrates answers old suspicions and formal charges by explaining his habit of questioning reputedly knowledgeable citizens.

structure.title: Penalty and departure
structure.text: The later speeches consider an appropriate penalty and address the people judging him. His manner remains part of the argument.

people.name: Socrates
people.text: A seventy-year-old Athenian philosopher on trial for impiety and corrupting the young, who uses his defence to explain the habit of questioning that made him enemies.

people.name: Meletus
people.text: A young poet who brings the formal charge against Socrates, and who is cross-examined so sharply that his own grasp of the accusation starts to slip.

people.name: The jury
people.text: Five hundred ordinary Athenian citizens who will vote on the verdict, and whom Socrates refuses to flatter, weep before, or beg.

context.title: Defence, not regret
context.text: The title means a speech in defence. Socrates is not promising the kind of apology that seeks forgiveness by admitting fault.

context.title: Plato's representation
context.text: Plato presents a philosophical portrait of the defence. Read it as a shaped account, not a modern court transcript.
context.takeaway: The form helps define Socrates' example.

notice.why: Socrates' distinction explains why his questioning provokes hostility.
His conduct tests the values he claims to defend.

passages.quote: so persuasively did they speak; and yet they have hardly uttered a word of truth.

opening: Socrates is on trial for his life, and a more accommodating defendant might apologise. Instead, he explains why Athens needs someone who keeps embarrassing its most confident citizens. He has spent years asking people to account for what they claim to know; now the city has the power to make him stop. Plato's account of his defence turns a courtroom into a final public demonstration of the habit under prosecution, with a verdict that matters considerably more than winning an argument.
